source.title: Data Budgeting for Machine Learning
source.authors: Xinyi Zhao; Weixin Liang; James Y. Zou

record.tranche_reason: Applies a power-law fitting baseline to data-versus-performance curves for tabular ML tasks and reports its prediction results in that new setting; it does not test language-model pretraining scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling work and evaluates a power-law baseline on tabular classification tasks. Its own results are aggregate predictions over tabular datasets, not measurements of language-model loss, parameter/token/compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: The study treats a power-law fit (f(x)=1−b·x^c) as a dataset-independent baseline for predicting tabular classification performance. It reports only that its own learning-based method beats this baseline. The learners are RandomForest/AutoML models on at most 2,500 tabular examples, not neural language-model pretraining or a neural regime covered by V5. No version names this setting. The study never measures how well a power law fits the learning curves, and it does not scale model size or compute. Its Powerlaw numbers are baseline comparisons, not tests of a scaling-law version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that learning from other datasets predicts final performance and needed data better than the dataset-independent Powerlaw method, especially with small pilot sets. They add that test-set size and label balance affect prediction quality.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a power-law fit to tabular task performance versus training-data size, with F1-based performance and pilot-data extrapolation; it does not measure language-model loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction results vary with pilot-data size; the authors also report effects from test-set size and label balance.

fits_no_version.finding: On 383 tabular datasets with RandomForest learners, a power-law fit to pilot learning curves predicts saturating F1 poorly with small pilots and better with larger ones. R2 is 0.17 at 50 points, 0.55 at 100 and 0.75 at 200. Learning-based predictors beat it at every pilot size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law extrapolation of small-sample learning curves predicts saturating performance of classical ML on tabular data.

record.problems: The results concern tabular datasets rather than language models. The reported table gives aggregate metrics without uncertainty estimates, and the paper notes that imbalanced datasets and limited pilot data can lead to inaccurate predictions.

untested.parts: All of it. No language-model loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All of it. Extrapolation runs only from ≤200 to 2,500 tabular examples; no LM runs.
Other neural modalities and regimes (image, video, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer). Tabular RandomForest curves are outside the version, and the study does not report power-law fit quality.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this study T3/tests V5. That is wrong: the power law is only a baseline the study's method is compared against. The setting is non-neural tabular classification measured with F1, which no version covers.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small language-model runs to runs orders of magnitude larger.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, including how either scales with compute.
Architecture effects at a fixed parameter count.
The paper tests a power-law baseline for tabular ML data scaling only; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or language-model pretraining.
Downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and bends in language-model scaling curves.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tabular ML benchmark at pilot sizes 50, 100, and 200
reader_labels.reason: The power-law baseline gives some final-performance prediction signal, but its results vary with pilot size and needed-data-bin accuracy remains low; the authors report that learning-based methods outperform it, especially for small pilots (r1-r6).
